content: Vertigo, arthralgia, myalgia, paresthesia, tremor, irritability, anxiety, pruritus, fatigue, somnolence, seizures, and syncope are potential adverse effects. Neutropenia and leukopenia have been reported. Hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, may occur. Vertigo and angioedema are possible side effects. Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) has been observed. Muscle weakness, amnesia, polyneuropathy, apathy, agitation, psychotic behavior, and sleep disorders may develop. Thrombocytopenia has been reported. Hypersensitivity to nifurtimox or any of its excipients is a contraindication. Alcohol consumption during treatment is not recommended. Genotoxicity has been demonstrated in humans, in vitro in several bacterial species and mammalian cell systems, and in vivo in rodents. A study in children treated for Chagas disease (aged 7 months to 14 years) showed a 13-fold increase in chromosomal aberrations. Carcinogenicity has been observed in mice and rats treated chronically with nitrofuran agents structurally similar to nifurtimox, though no similar data have been reported for nifurtimox itself. The association with carcinogenicity remains unknown. Nifurtimox may cause fetal harm when administered to pregnant females. Patients with a history of brain injury, seizures, psychiatric disease, or serious behavioral alterations may experience worsening of their conditions; close monitoring is required for these patients and for those who develop neurological disturbances or psychiatric drug reactions during treatment. Hypersensitivity reactions have been reported, which may be induced by nifurtimox or an immune response triggered by Chagas disease during treatment. Treatment should be discontinued at the first sign of serious hypersensitivity. Decreased appetite and weight loss have been reported. Patients may lose their appetite or experience nausea/vomiting, leading to weight loss. Body weight should be checked every 14 days, and the dose should be adjusted accordingly. Nitrofuran derivatives may precipitate acute attacks of porphyria. Tablets should be administered under close medical supervision in patients with porphyria. Based on animal studies, nifurtimox may cause fetal harm when administered to pregnant females. Published postmarketing reports on use during pregnancy are insufficient to inform a drug-associated risk of birth defects and miscarriage. A pregnancy test is recommended before initiating treatment. Published literature demonstrates that nifurtimox is present in human breast milk, with an estimated infant daily dose of less than 15% of the recommended daily dose for pediatric patients with Chagas disease. No adverse effects have been reported in the small number of infants who were breastfed by treated mothers. There is no information on the effects of nifurtimox on milk production. Infants exposed to the drug should be monitored for vomiting, rash, decreased appetite, pyrexia, and irritability. Nifurtimox is generally acceptable for use. Controlled studies in pregnant women show no evidence of fetal risk. Approximately 44% of the drug is excreted in urine in the fed state and 27% in the fasted state, primarily as metabolites. Nifurtimox should be administered with food. Tablets are functionally scored and may be split into halves (e.g., 15 mg and 60 mg) at scored lines by hand. Tablets should not be broken mechanically with a tablet-splitting device. Store nifurtimox at controlled room temperature (20–25°C or 68–77°F), with excursions permitted to 15–30°C (59–86°F). Tablets should be stored in the original bottle with child-resistant closures, and the desiccant should not be removed. Keep the bottle tightly closed and protect it from moisture. Adding plans allows for comparison of formulary status with other drugs in the same class. Formulary information may vary and is subject to change. Contact the applicable plan provider for the most current information. The recipient of this information will receive further details and instructions to access the offer.
